title: Bunk Johnson in New Orleans and in the 1940s comeback
summary: He heard Bunk as a child and again in 1945; the 1940s band kept the old style, with George Lewis and the Marrero family.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: You were talking about Armstrong, Albert. Yeah. And remember you saying the other day that you thought that Louis got a lot from Bunk and those more recent records made in American music by Bunk, you didn't feel were really Bunk in his prime. Obviously they weren't because he was getting on years. Could you tell us a bit about Bunk? You heard Bunk in New Orleans.

When I first heard Bunk, I was a kid around nine or ten years old. He was playing with the Superior Band. Maggill was playing with the Imperial. Bunk was the radiest trumpet player at that time in New Orleans, what we call Gut Bucket later on. He was a kid around nine or ten years old. He was a writer. And Bunk had ideas. It's too bad that they weren't recording in those times. This man was really great. And I heard the old man again in 45, after being in retirement for 20-some years, and 60-some years of age. He made a remarkable comeback. But that wasn't the same Bunk I knew. No.
Would you say that that band that was recorded in 42, 43, 44, the Bunk band, it was the same as Bunk was playing around about 1918?

The style was the same because he got all the old musicians to play that style, like George Lewis and his guitar player. His old man used to play bass. What's his name? Schlerdragpa? No, no, no, Morera. Lawrence Morera. Yeah, I know his brother John and Simon were the two greatest string men we had. He played with the Young Olympia Band in 17, 18, 19 and 20 like that. Morera was a kid. He was a little younger than I am. He was small. His old man was a hell of a bass player. And when they got this band for Bunk, George Lewis was playing on this old style, as real New Orleans, as authentic. He had never left New Orleans, you know what I mean, to play in other styles. And it was really an old New Orleans thing. It was wonderful to hear someone still playing it, you know what I mean? Because we didn't hear it in New York and Chicago. These guys were playing something else.
